issue_context.title: ENH: Support Left Semi Joins
issue_context.body:
#### Is your feature request related to a problem?

I wish I could use the Pandas `DataFrame.join` function to perform left semi joins: selecting each row from the left DataFrame that has at least one matching row in the right DataFrame.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like to be able to pass `leftsemi` to the `how` parameter in the `DataDrame.join` function to perform this type of join.

#### Additional context

For example: in SQL this might look like

```SQL
SELECT *
FROM table1
WHERE EXISTS
(SELECT 1
FROM   table2
WHERE  table1.id = table2.id)
```
comments: this is just a join after you isin on the rhs - would take a PR for this naive implementation
If there are duplicate matches on the RHS, I think a left semijoin would only produce a single row. But I think this can be produced with a drop duplicates on the left columns.

Hi I would like to work on this enhancement, if no one is working on this. 
I have few questions:
1) Incase of column name mentioned in 'on' param provided, a .isin must be performed on the same 'on' value in rhs df right for the unique values of the 'on' column in lhs?.
2) If no 'on' param value is provided, then the isin should be performed on the index of the rhs?
3) The columns of the rhs dataframe present in the resulting dataframe from .join be dropped? Because the query selects only the rows in lhs df for which there are matching rows in rhs df.

Hi @aneesh98, just wanted to check if you are working on this?
Otherwise I would like to pick this up.
Hi @debnathshoham, I am actually still working on it.

Great!
To answer the questions above:
1. Correct
2. Merge can happen using `on`, `left_on` & `right_on`, `right_index` & `left_index`, `left_index` & `right_on` and `right_index` & `left_on`. If none of these are provided, it tries `on` the common columns.
3. AFAIU semi join should only returns rows from `left` that has matching rows in `right`. It won't add columns from `right`.

Hope that helps.

Hi @debnathshoham. Thank you so much for reply.
Can you please confirm if this approach is correct then?
1) If 'on' is None and join is to be done on index-to-index, then find out the rows present in the left dataframe which have matching index values in the right dataframe
2) If 'on' is provided, then perform an inner join based on the values provided in 'on', discard the columns from right dataframe and remove duplicates.

Please let me know if I am correct with this logic, or if I am missing any case or anything at all?. Thank you.

>Merge can happen using on, left_on & right_on, right_index & left_index, left_index & right_on and right_index & left_on. If none of these are provided, it tries on the common columns.

Yes, actually you have just considered 2 cases from  the 5 I mentioned (you will get a clear picture, if you play around with all these existing merging procedures). 

The idea is really simple, in `leftsemi`, check for the keys in `left` (can be either index(s) or column(s)) `isin` the keys in the `right` (again, could be either index(s) or column(s)). And return those keys from `left`.

You can check this example from [stack](https://stackoverflow.com/a/43099771/4236684). Hope this will clarify.

review_comments: What's the performance of this? Say you have two large frames (maybe check 10k and 100k rows) that have the same result whether it be a left or leftsemi (I think e.g. the keys being unique guarantees this), how does the performance compare?

> that have the same result whether it be a left or leftsemi

I will have to check that, but doesn't `leftsemi` just return the left df, nothing from the right df?
Ah, when I said "same result" above, I was merely thinking that the left join won't produce duplicate rows (so the results are the same length). You're correct the results won't be the same.

```python
left = pd.DataFrame({"a":range(100000), "b":["a","b","c","d"]*25000})
right = pd.DataFrame({"a":range(100000), "b":["d","e","f", "g"]*25000})
%timeit left.merge(right)
41 ms ± 321 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
%timeit left.merge(right, how="leftsemi")
63.9 ms ± 2.55 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

Thanks! `merge` will use all columns that are in common by default, your example is an empty result. While informative, I think a non-empty result is probably more common for testing.

I'm seeing this is faster (for this particular example which _may_ be too simple) on one column, and ~5x slower once you get to four or more. While there may be opportunities for better performance, that seems reasonable for a new feature.

<details>
<summary>Code</summary>

```
for n_columns in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
    on = list(range(n_columns))
    left = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            **{i: range(100000) for i in on},
            **{"values":["a","b","c","d"]*25000},
        }
    )
    right = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            **{i: range(100000) for i in on},
            **{"values":["d","e","f", "g"]*25000},
        }
    )

    print(f'{n_columns=}')
    %timeit left.merge(right, on=on)
    %timeit left.merge(right, on=on, how="leftsemi")
    print('---')
```

</details>

Any suggestions how performance can be improved?

No, not offhand. Just to show there is room for performance improvement, here is a hacky solution (won't work in all cases):

```
def my_leftsemi(left, right, on):
    right = right.drop(columns='values')
    left['left_row'] = range(len(left))
    left['index'] = left.index
    result = (
        left.merge(right, on=on)
        .drop_duplicates(subset='left_row')
        .drop(columns='left_row')
    )
    result = result.set_index('index').sort_index()
    result.index.name = None
    return result
```

This produces the same result, and has runtime similar to the current left join on many columns. The 2nd line for each time is the method implemented in this PR, the third line is `my_leftsemi`.

Thanks @rhshadrach for the review.

I took a look into `leftsemi` and it is taking long because of the use of `isin` (I think that was suggested in a comment in the bug report).
We can implement `leftsemi` without using `isin` too (something similar to your `my_leftsemi` func). But I think that would get more complicated if we try to cover all the use cases. Let me know if you think I should take this PR towards that direction.

Digressing a little from above, I also tried another use case perf. I changed it a little (output lens are still same), and the perf diff has changed significantly in the opposite direction.

Let me know your thoughts.

<details>
<summary>Code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
for n_columns in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
    on = list(range(n_columns))
    left = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            **{"l"+str(i): range(100000) for i in on},
            **{"values_l":["a","b","c","d"]*25000},
            **{"key": range(2, 100002)}
        }
    )
    right = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            **{"r"+str(i): range(100000) for i in on},
            **{"values_r":["d","e","f", "g"]*25000},
            **{"key": range(100000)}
        }
    )
    print(f'{n_columns=}')
    %timeit left.merge(right)
    %timeit left.merge(right, how="leftsemi")
    print('---')
```
</details>

> We can implement `leftsemi` without using `isin` too (something similar to your `my_leftsemi` func). But I think that would get more complicated if we try to cover all the use cases. Let me know if you think I should take this PR towards that direction.

I don't think this should go in that direction unless there already is a viable alternative; to my knowledge there isn't. As I remarked above, while this performance is less than left-join on my columns, I feel it's sufficient for the feature.

> Digressing a little from above, I also tried another use case perf. I changed it a little (output lens are still same), and the perf diff has changed significantly in the opposite direction.

Left join has to take all the columns from right where as leftsemi does not. In other words, these operations in this case are quite different, so I don't think it's meaningful to compare. Also, perhaps I didn't highlight this well enough, but joining on 1-3 columns is either significantly faster or comparable to left joins. In my experience this is the common case; I can't remember the last time I joined on 10 columns :laughing:

> Left join has to take all the columns from right where as leftsemi does not

Rational behind this test was, I think that's the use case where someone would use `leftsemi` join.
But yes, I do agree that since the output is widely different, this is not fair to `leftjoin`.
